stem: An analyst wants the `cust_sgnup_dt` field to read Signup Date everywhere in Tableau. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Select the field in the Data pane, press F2 and type the new name
options.rationale: F2 (or right-click > Rename) makes the field name editable in the Data pane.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Aliases, then type Signup Date
options.rationale: Aliases relabel the members of a dimension, not the field itself.

options.text: Open the source CSV and change the column header, then reconnect
options.rationale: This edits the source, which is unnecessary. Tableau renames fields as metadata.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Default Properties > Comment
options.rationale: A comment is a note in the field's tooltip. It doesn't change the name.

explanation: Fields are renamed directly in the Data pane (F2, or right-click > Rename). Only what appears in Tableau changes. The source stays as it is.

stem: After renaming a field in the Data pane, what happens in the underlying data source?

options.text: The column header in the source file is rewritten to match the new name
options.rationale: Tableau never writes back to the source when a field is renamed.

options.text: The rename applies only until the workbook is closed
options.rationale: The new name is saved with the workbook.

options.text: Nothing: only the name shown in Tableau changes
options.rationale: Renaming is metadata. The source keeps its original column name.

options.text: Tableau stores the new name only if the data is first extracted
options.rationale: Renames are kept whether the source is live or an extract.

explanation: A rename changes what appears in Tableau. It is saved with the workbook and when the data source is exported, but the source itself is untouched.

stem: An analyst renamed `Device` to Playback Device by mistake and wants the original name back. What is the quickest way?

options.text: Rename the field again and type the original name from memory
options.rationale: This can work, but it is the slow path and risks a typo.

options.text: Click the circular arrow in the edit box to restore the name
options.rationale: The restore arrow resets the field to its original data-source name.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Clear Aliases
options.rationale: Clear Aliases resets member labels. It doesn't touch the field name.

options.text: Delete the field and reconnect to the data source
options.rationale: Nothing needs to be deleted. Reconnecting is unnecessary and can break views.

explanation: While a name is being edited, a small circular arrow restores the original data-source field name. Reset Names does the same for several fields at once.

stem: An analyst has renamed eight fields in the Data pane and wants them all back to their source names. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Select the fields and choose Clear Aliases from the right-click menu
options.rationale: Aliases belong to members. They have nothing to do with field names.

options.text: Open each field's Default Properties and set the name there
options.rationale: Default Properties set number format, color, sort and so on, not the name.

options.text: Re-import the file as a new data source and republish
options.rationale: A new source is overkill and would discard the other work in the workbook.

options.text: Select the fields, right-click and choose Reset Names
options.rationale: Reset Names restores every selected field to its original name in one step.

explanation: Select several fields, right-click and choose Reset Names to undo renames in bulk. For a single field, use the restore arrow in its edit box.

stem: A team lead exports a data source after renaming fields in it. A colleague opens the exported data source. Which field names does the colleague see?

options.text: The original source column names, because renames never leave the workbook
options.rationale: Renames are saved in the export too.

options.text: The renamed fields, but only if the data was extracted first
options.rationale: An extract is not required for names to be saved.

options.text: The renamed fields, because renames are saved with the export
options.rationale: The changed name is saved with the workbook and when you export the data source.

options.text: A prompt asking which version of each name to keep
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't ask. The exported source carries the new names.

explanation: A field rename is stored as metadata, so it travels with the workbook and with an exported data source. That is why renaming is safe to do once for a whole team.

stem: Which change is a rename of a field rather than an alias, a data type change or a default property?

options.text: `Device` is shown as Playback Device in the Data pane and in every view
options.rationale: Only the field's own name changes. That is a rename.

options.text: The `PRM` plan code is displayed as Premium in every view
options.rationale: That relabels one member of a dimension. It is an alias.

options.text: `Postal Code` is converted from a number to a text string
options.rationale: That is a data type change.

options.text: `Monthly Price` always appears with a currency number format
options.rationale: That is a default property (number format).

explanation: Renaming changes the field's name. Aliases change member labels, data types change how values are read, and default properties set how a field behaves when used.

stem: Which two statements about renaming a field in the Data pane are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It changes only what appears in Tableau, not the underlying data source
options.rationale: The source column keeps its original name.

options.text: The field's name in the source database is renamed to match
options.rationale: Tableau never writes the new name back to the source.

options.text: The new name is saved with the workbook
options.rationale: Renames are stored with the workbook and with exported data sources.

options.text: It can only be done on the Data Source page
options.rationale: Fields are renamed right in the Data pane of a worksheet.

options.text: It also relabels every member of the field
options.rationale: Member labels are changed with aliases.

explanation: A rename is workbook metadata: it changes the displayed field name, is saved with the workbook and never touches the source.

stem: Which two actions let an analyst rename a field in the Data pane? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Select the field and press F2
options.rationale: F2 makes the name editable.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Aliases
options.rationale: Aliases relabel members, not the field.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Default Properties > Number Format
options.rationale: That sets how numbers display.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Rename
options.rationale: Rename opens the name for editing.

options.text: Click the data type icon and choose Geographic Role
options.rationale: That assigns a map role.

explanation: In the Data pane, select a field and press F2 or right-click and choose Rename, then type the new name. The other menus set member labels, formats or roles.

stem: Which three statements about restoring renamed fields are true? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: The circular arrow in a field's edit box restores its original name
options.rationale: It brings back the original data-source name.

options.text: Reset Names restores the original names of several selected fields at once
options.rationale: Select the fields, right-click and choose Reset Names.

options.text: Resetting a name writes the old name back into the source file
options.rationale: Tableau never changes the source, so there is nothing to write back.

options.text: Clear Aliases restores renamed fields to their original names
options.rationale: Clear Aliases resets member labels only.

options.text: Resetting a name deletes the field from the workbook
options.rationale: The field stays. Only its displayed name returns to the original.

options.text: The original name that comes back is the field name from the data source
options.rationale: The restore uses the name from the underlying source.

explanation: Tableau remembers the source field name, so you can restore it with the edit-box arrow or Reset Names. Neither affects aliases or the data itself.

stem: Plan codes `BAS`, `STD` and `PRM` should read Basic, Standard and Premium in views. Where does the analyst set this?

options.text: Right-click `Plan Code` and choose Rename
options.rationale: Rename changes the field's name, not its members' labels.

options.text: Right-click `Plan Code` in the Data pane and choose Aliases
options.rationale: The Aliases dialog lists each member with a box for its new label.

options.text: Click the data type icon of `Plan Code` and choose a new data type
options.rationale: The data type controls how values are read, not how they are labeled.

options.text: Right-click `Plan Code` and choose Default Properties > Sort
options.rationale: Sort sets member order, not the labels.

explanation: Aliases are alternate names for members of a dimension. They are edited in the Aliases dialog, opened from the dimension's right-click menu in the Data pane.

stem: Which of these fields can have aliases assigned to its members?

options.text: `Minutes Watched`, a measure
options.rationale: Measures can't be aliased, because that would modify data values.

options.text: `Start`, used as a continuous date
options.rationale: Aliases can't be created for dates or continuous fields.

options.text: `Device`, a discrete dimension
options.rationale: Aliases work on members of discrete dimensions.

options.text: `Monthly Price`, a measure
options.rationale: Measures can't be aliased.

explanation: Only discrete dimensions have members that can be relabeled. Measures, dates and continuous fields can't be aliased.

stem: An analyst set aliases on `Plan Code` and now wants every member to show its original value again. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Choose Reset Names from the field's right-click menu
options.rationale: Reset Names restores field names, not member labels.

options.text: Edit the plan codes in the source file
options.rationale: The source was never changed by the aliases.

options.text: Change the field's data type to string and back
options.rationale: The data type has no effect on aliases.

options.text: Open the Aliases dialog and choose Clear Aliases
options.rationale: Clear Aliases sets the members back to their original names.

explanation: Clear Aliases in the Aliases dialog removes the alternate labels. Reset Names is the equivalent for renamed fields.

stem: The `City` field lists both Cologne and Köln for the same place. The analyst wants one combined mark. What is the right approach?

options.text: Create a group of the two members
options.rationale: A group combines several members into one, which an alias can't do.

options.text: Give Köln the alias Cologne in the Aliases dialog
options.rationale: An alias only changes a label. The two members stay separate.

options.text: Rename the `City` field to Cologne
options.rationale: Renaming the field changes its name, not its members.

options.text: Assign the City geographic role to the field
options.rationale: The role maps values but doesn't merge spellings.

explanation: Aliases relabel a single member and can't merge two of them. To combine spellings of one place, build a group on the field.

stem: A workbook connects to a published data source. What does Tableau allow regarding aliases there?

options.text: Aliases can be created, but only on measures
options.rationale: Measures can never be aliased.

options.text: Aliases can be created and are saved to the published source
options.rationale: They can't be created here at all.

options.text: Aliases can be created but only for continuous dimensions
options.rationale: Continuous fields can't be aliased.

options.text: Aliases can't be created or edited on a published data source
options.rationale: Aliases are a property of the data source definition, so a published one is locked.

explanation: When using a published data source, you can't create or edit aliases there. Edits to member labels belong to whoever owns the published source.

stem: What exactly does an alias change when `PRM` is given the alias Premium?

options.text: The name of the `Plan Code` field in the Data pane
options.rationale: That would be a rename.

options.text: The label that members of that dimension show in the view
options.rationale: An alias is a display label for one member.

options.text: The `PRM` value stored in the source data
options.rationale: Aliases never modify the data values.

options.text: The data type of every plan in the field
options.rationale: Data types are changed from the type icon.

explanation: An alias relabels a member, not the field and not the data. The source still holds `PRM`.

stem: Which two Driftlight fields can have their members aliased? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `Minutes Watched`, a measure
options.rationale: Measures can't be aliased.

options.text: `Plan Code`, a discrete dimension
options.rationale: Its members, codes such as `BAS` and `PRM`, can get readable labels.

options.text: `Start`, used as a continuous date
options.rationale: Continuous dates can't be aliased.

options.text: `Device`, a discrete dimension
options.rationale: Members such as TV and Web can be relabeled.

options.text: `Monthly Price`, a measure
options.rationale: Measures can't be aliased.

explanation: Discrete dimensions have members that can be relabeled. Measures and continuous fields can't have aliases.

stem: Which two statements about aliases are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Right-click a dimension in the Data pane and choose Aliases to edit them
options.rationale: That opens the dialog listing the members.

options.text: An alias can be created for a measure
options.rationale: Aliasing would modify data values, which Tableau doesn't allow.

options.text: Two members can be merged into one by giving them the same alias
options.rationale: Merging members is done with a group.

options.text: Clear Aliases sets the members back to their original names
options.rationale: It removes the alternate labels.

options.text: Aliases can be edited in a published data source
options.rationale: They can't be created or edited there.

explanation: Aliases are edited from the dimension's right-click menu and cleared with Clear Aliases. They are limited to discrete dimensions and unavailable in published sources.

stem: Which three fields are suitable for aliasing to make their members easier to read? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: `Device`
options.rationale: A discrete dimension, so its members can be relabeled.

options.text: `Monthly Price`
options.rationale: A measure, which can't be aliased.

options.text: `Latitude`
options.rationale: A measure by default, so it can't be aliased.

options.text: `Plan Code`
options.rationale: A discrete dimension whose codes benefit from readable labels.

options.text: `Channel`
options.rationale: A discrete dimension with text members.

options.text: `Minutes Watched`
options.rationale: A measure, which can't be aliased.

explanation: Only discrete dimensions can be aliased. Text fields such as `Plan Code`, `Device` and `Channel` qualify. Numeric measures don't.

stem: How does an analyst assign a geographic role to the `Country` field?

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Aliases, then pick Country/Region
options.rationale: Aliases relabel members and have no roles.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Default Properties > Shape on the menu
options.rationale: Shape sets member shapes, not a map role.

options.text: Click the data type icon, choose Geographic Role, then the role
options.rationale: The role lives in the same menu as the data type.

options.text: Drag the field to the Marks card and choose Geographic Role
options.rationale: The role is set in the Data pane. Dragging only places the field.

explanation: In the Data pane, click the field's data type icon, select Geographic Role and choose the role. The field's icon then becomes a globe.

stem: After the Country/Region role is assigned to `Country`, which fields does Tableau add to the Data pane?

options.text: `Country (Map)` and `Country (Region)` in the dimensions area
options.rationale: Tableau adds no such fields.

options.text: `Latitude (generated)` and `Longitude (generated)` in the measures area
options.rationale: These generated measures hold the coordinates for the map.

options.text: `Latitude` and `Longitude` columns written into the source file
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't change the source. The coordinates are generated fields.

options.text: A new calculated field named `Country (Role)`
options.rationale: No calculated field is created.

explanation: Assigning a geographic role makes Tableau generate Latitude and Longitude as measures, so the values can be placed on a map.

stem: A `Country` field already has the Country/Region role. How does the analyst get a map view?

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Convert to Map
options.rationale: There is no such command.

options.text: Add the field to Filters and choose Map
options.rationale: Filtering doesn't build a map.

options.text: Change the field's data type to Boolean
options.rationale: Types don't create views. A Boolean has nothing to place on a map.

options.text: Add the field to Detail on the Marks card
options.rationale: Tableau creates a map view when a geographic field goes on Detail.

explanation: With a geographic role in place, adding the field to Detail on the Marks card produces a map view with the generated Latitude and Longitude.

stem: For which kind of field are the Latitude and Longitude geographic roles available?

options.text: Numeric fields
options.rationale: The Latitude and Longitude roles are only available for numeric fields.

options.text: Text fields only
options.rationale: A text field holds names such as cities and gets roles like City.

options.text: Date fields only
options.rationale: Dates have no coordinate meaning.

options.text: Any field that is a discrete dimension
options.rationale: Being discrete isn't the requirement. The values have to be numbers.

explanation: Coordinates are numbers, so the Latitude and Longitude roles can only be assigned to numeric fields.

stem: Which two things happen after the Country/Region role is assigned to the `Country` field? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The field's icon changes to a globe
options.rationale: The globe marks geographic values used with maps.

options.text: The country names in the source file are replaced with ISO codes
options.rationale: Tableau never changes the source data.

options.text: `Latitude (generated)` and `Longitude (generated)` appear in the measures
options.rationale: These hold the generated coordinates.

options.text: The field is converted into a measure
options.rationale: It stays a dimension.

options.text: A map is drawn automatically on the Rows shelf
options.rationale: A map appears when the field is added to Detail on the Marks card.

explanation: A geographic role changes the field's icon to a globe and generates Latitude and Longitude measures. A map appears once the field is placed on Detail.

stem: A map of Driftlight subscribers shows a note in the lower right corner saying some values are unknown. What should the analyst do first?

options.text: Remove the geographic field from Detail on the Marks card
options.rationale: This hides the problem, and the map is lost. The unknown values still need a fix.

options.text: Click the note and choose Edit Locations
options.rationale: Edit Locations is where unrecognized values can be matched or given coordinates.

options.text: Assign the Latitude role to the field
options.rationale: The Latitude and Longitude roles are only for numeric fields and don't resolve unmatched text.

options.text: Create aliases for the unknown members in the Aliases dialog
options.rationale: Aliases only change display labels. They don't tell Tableau where a place is.

explanation: When Tableau can't match some values to a location, it flags them as unknown on the map. The indicator opens Edit Locations (also under the Map menu), where the analyst can match values, add a field or enter coordinates.

stem: A `City` field contains the value Paris, and Tableau can't tell whether it means Paris, France or Paris, Texas. How can the analyst remove the ambiguity?

options.text: Rename the field to Paris City in the Data pane
options.rationale: Renaming changes only the field name, not how Tableau matches places.

options.text: Change the data type of `City` to Number
options.rationale: A place name is text. A number type would turn the values into Null.

options.text: In Edit Locations, add a Country or State field to the match
options.rationale: A parent field gives Tableau enough context to pick the right place.

options.text: Assign the Airport role to `City`
options.rationale: The role changes how values are matched, but it doesn't add the context that separates two Paris entries.

explanation: Ambiguous place names are resolved in Edit Locations by adding a Country or State field. Tableau then matches each city within its country or state.

stem: Which two things can an analyst do in the Edit Locations dialog? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Match values Tableau doesn't recognize to known locations
options.rationale: Matching unrecognized values to known ones is a core use of the dialog.

options.text: Merge two spellings of a city into one member
options.rationale: Merging members needs a group, not Edit Locations.

options.text: Set the default sort order for the field
options.rationale: Sort is a default property in the Data pane.

options.text: Enter latitude and longitude for a value by hand
options.rationale: Manual coordinates are allowed for values that can't be matched.

options.text: Change the field's data type to string
options.rationale: Data types are changed from the type icon.

explanation: Edit Locations handles unknown or ambiguous places: add a Country or State field, match unrecognized values, or type in coordinates. Merging members or changing types are separate tools.

stem: The `Postal Code` field has been changed to a string. What should the analyst do next so Tableau can place the codes on a map?

options.text: Assign the Longitude role from the data type icon
options.rationale: Longitude is for numeric fields and a postal code isn't a coordinate.

options.text: Set Default Properties > Number Format on the field
options.rationale: Number formats apply to numbers and don't tell Tableau where a code is.

options.text: Add an alias for each postal code
options.rationale: Aliases only relabel members and don't give them a location.

options.text: Assign the ZIP Code/Postcode geographic role from the data type icon
options.rationale: The role lets Tableau recognize the strings as postal codes.

explanation: A string type keeps leading zeros intact, and the ZIP Code/Postcode role is what makes Tableau treat the values as places. Both steps are done from the data type icon.

stem: Where can an analyst change the data type of a field in the Data pane?

options.text: Click the icon to the left of the field name and pick a type from the list
options.rationale: The type icon opens the data type choices.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Aliases
options.rationale: Aliases rename members and don't alter the type.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Default Properties
options.rationale: Defaults cover formats and aggregation, not the data type.

options.text: Double-click the field name
options.rationale: Double-clicking doesn't offer type choices.

explanation: The icon beside a field shows its type, and clicking it lists the other types. Changing the type is metadata, so the source stays as it is.

stem: An analyst is already looking at a worksheet and spots a numeric field that should be text. Which route changes the type from the view?

options.text: Drag the field onto the Detail card
options.rationale: Detail changes the level of detail and not the type.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Change Data Type
options.rationale: The context menu on the field includes Change Data Type.

options.text: Open Analysis > Create Calculated Field and retype the name
options.rationale: A calculation creates a new field and doesn't convert the original.

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Clear Aliases
options.rationale: This resets member labels. It doesn't change a type.

explanation: A field's data type can be changed in the Data pane, on the Data Source page, or by right-clicking a field and choosing Change Data Type.

stem: Newark's postal code `07106` was read from a file as a number. What is the result?

options.text: It stays 07106, but it can't be placed on a map
options.rationale: The leading zero is lost when the value is read as a number.

options.text: It becomes Null, because numbers can't hold five digits
options.rationale: Five digits fit in a number type, and the value is only reshaped.

options.text: It shows as 7106, and Tableau offers to aggregate the codes
options.rationale: A number drops the leading zero and behaves like a measure.

options.text: It is split into 07 and 106 as two fields
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't split values by type.

explanation: Read as a number, a code loses its leading zero and Tableau treats it as something to sum. Postal codes should be strings.

stem: A column mixes numbers with a few text entries such as n/a, and the field's type is Number. How does Tableau treat the text entries?

options.text: As zero
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't convert text to zero.

options.text: As the largest number in the column
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't assign values to text this way.

options.text: As text, shown in the view next to the numbers
options.rationale: A number field can't hold text members, so they don't appear as text.

options.text: As Null
options.rationale: With a number type, text is treated as Null.

explanation: Values that don't fit the field's type become Null. Changing a field to a type that can't hold its values loses them in the view.

stem: An analyst needs to fix a wrong data type and also plans to create an extract. When should the type be changed?

options.text: Before creating the extract
options.rationale: Types should be right before the extract is built.

options.text: After creating the extract, from the extract's page
options.rationale: Changing types afterwards is the wrong order. Do it first.

options.text: It doesn't matter, because extracts always re-read types
options.rationale: Extracts store the data as prepared, so the order matters.

options.text: Only in the source file, never in Tableau
options.rationale: Tableau can change types itself as metadata.

explanation: Change data types before creating an extract. It's the order Tableau's documentation recommends.

stem: On the Data Source page, how does an analyst change the type of a field in the grid?

options.text: Double-click a cell and type the new type name
options.rationale: Cells hold data and don't set the type.

options.text: Click the data type icon above the field and choose a type
options.rationale: The icon in the grid header opens the type list.

options.text: Open the Map menu and choose Edit Locations
options.rationale: Edit Locations handles map locations only.

options.text: Drag the field to the Filters shelf
options.rationale: Filters limit rows. They don't change the type.

explanation: The Data Source page shows a type icon for every field. Click it to pick another type.

stem: Which two places let an analyst change a field's data type? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The Marks card
options.rationale: The Marks card holds encodings and doesn't offer data types.

options.text: The Data Source page grid
options.rationale: The icon above each column opens the type list.

options.text: The Aliases dialog
options.rationale: Aliases are for member labels.

options.text: The Data pane in a worksheet
options.rationale: The icon next to a field name offers the same choice.

options.text: The Format pane
options.rationale: Formatting changes appearance only.

explanation: Types can be changed on the Data Source page, in the Data pane, or via right-click > Change Data Type in a view.

stem: A source file contains postal codes such as `07106`. Which two steps should the analyst take? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Alias each code with its city
options.rationale: Aliases don't fix the type.

options.text: Set the aggregation to Sum
options.rationale: Postal codes shouldn't be added up.

options.text: Change the field to a string
options.rationale: A string keeps the leading zero.

options.text: Leave the type as Number so the codes sort correctly
options.rationale: A number drops the leading zero.

options.text: Give the field the ZIP Code/Postcode role
options.rationale: The role lets Tableau map the values.

explanation: Postal codes are labels, not quantities. A string type protects the leading zero, and the ZIP Code/Postcode role makes them mappable.

stem: Which three data types can the type icon of a field show in Tableau? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Date & time
options.rationale: Date & time is one of the types.

options.text: Currency
options.rationale: Currency is a number format, not a data type.

options.text: Boolean
options.rationale: True/false values have their own type.

options.text: Hyperlink
options.rationale: Hyperlinks aren't a data type in the Data pane.

options.text: Number (decimal)
options.rationale: Numbers are whole or decimal.

explanation: Types are text (string), date, date & time, number, Boolean and geographic. Currency is a Default Property for formatting numbers.

stem: An analyst wants `Monthly Price` to show as currency with two decimals in every future view. Where should that be set?

options.text: Format the pill in one worksheet
options.rationale: That changes only the one sheet.

options.text: Create an alias for each price
options.rationale: Aliases don't apply to measures.

options.text: Right-click the field in the Data pane and choose Default Properties > Number Format
options.rationale: Default properties apply whenever the field is dragged into a view.

options.text: Rename the field to Monthly Price (USD)
options.rationale: The name changes, but the format doesn't.

explanation: Defaults set in the Data pane apply to new views. Formatting a pill only affects the sheet in question.

stem: Which default property sets the colour of each `Plan` member whenever the field is placed on Color?

options.text: Default Properties > Aggregation
options.rationale: Aggregation is for measures.

options.text: Default Properties > Comment
options.rationale: A comment is just a tooltip note.

options.text: Default Properties > Number Format
options.rationale: Number formats are for numbers.

options.text: Default Properties > Color
options.rationale: The default colour assignment follows the field.

explanation: A dimension's Color default fixes each member's colour so it stays the same everywhere the field is used on Color.

stem: An analyst wants a measure to be totalled with AVG instead of SUM the first time it is dragged into a view. Which default property does this?

options.text: Aggregation
options.rationale: The default aggregation is used when the measure is first totaled.

options.text: Number Format
options.rationale: This controls how the result looks.

options.text: Comment
options.rationale: This adds a note and doesn't change the calculation.

options.text: Sort
options.rationale: Sort orders dimension members.

explanation: Aggregation is a default property for measures. It sets the aggregation used when the measure is first added.

stem: An analyst sets a default Sort on the `Genre` dimension. Besides how members are ordered in a view, what else does it control?

options.text: Which colour each member receives
options.rationale: Colours come from the Color default.

options.text: How the values are listed in a filter
options.rationale: The default sort also orders the filter's list.

options.text: Whether the field counts as a measure
options.rationale: The sort doesn't change a field's role.

options.text: The field's data type
options.rationale: Types are changed separately.

explanation: The default sort controls member order in views and also how the field's values are listed in a filter.

stem: After an analyst formats a pill on one worksheet as a percentage, a colleague drags the same field into a new worksheet. What do they see?

options.text: The percentage format, because formatting follows the field everywhere
options.rationale: That only happens if it was set as a default property.

options.text: An error, until the formats are reconciled
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't raise errors for this.

options.text: The format from the field's default properties, not the pill's
options.rationale: Pill formatting stays on its sheet.

options.text: A blank pill, until a default is chosen
options.rationale: The field simply uses its defaults.

explanation: Formatting in a view is local to that sheet. Defaults in the Data pane apply to every new view.

stem: Where does an analyst leave a note that appears in the Data pane tooltip of a field?

options.text: Aliases
options.rationale: Aliases relabel members.

options.text: Rename
options.rationale: Rename changes the field name.

options.text: Default Properties > Sort
options.rationale: Sort orders members.

options.text: Default Properties > Comment
options.rationale: Comments are available for any field.

explanation: The Comment property attaches a note to a field and shows it in the field's tooltip.

stem: Which three default properties are available for a measure like `Monthly Price`? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Shape
options.rationale: Shape is for dimensions.

options.text: Comment
options.rationale: Comments are available for any field.

options.text: Number Format
options.rationale: It applies to numbers.

options.text: Aggregation
options.rationale: The default aggregation is for measures.

options.text: Sort
options.rationale: Sort sets the default order of a dimension's members.

explanation: Comment works on any field, Number Format on numbers and Aggregation on measures. Sort and Shape are set per member, so they belong to dimensions.

stem: Which two default properties does Tableau apply to the members of `Plan` when the field goes on the matching Marks card shelf? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Aggregation
options.rationale: Aggregation is for measures.

options.text: Number Format
options.rationale: Number formats are for numbers.

options.text: Color
options.rationale: A colour for each member.

options.text: Date Format
options.rationale: Date formats are for dates.

options.text: Shape
options.rationale: A shape for each member.

explanation: Dimension defaults for Color and Shape take effect when the field is on Color or Shape.

stem: Which two statements about default properties and formatting are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Default properties rewrite the values in the source file
options.rationale: Defaults are metadata.

options.text: Formatting a single pill on a shelf changes only that sheet
options.rationale: Local formatting stays local.

options.text: A default is applied only to the first view of a workbook
options.rationale: Defaults apply to every new view.

options.text: Colour encodings are shared across worksheets using the same data source
options.rationale: Colour defaults are shared.

options.text: Defaults can be set only for measures
options.rationale: They also cover dimensions and dates.

explanation: Default Properties are stored in Tableau and shape each new view. Local formatting remains local.
